title: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter

instructions: Practice set for this lesson in the question types of the April 2026 paper.
Where a question has OR, answer either one.
Questions from previous NIOS papers show the exam they appeared in.

questions.q: A proton, a neutron, an electron and an α-particle have the same kinetic energy. Their de Broglie wavelengths compare as —
questions.answer: B
questions.work:
λ = h/√(2mK). With K equal, λ ∝ 1/√m.
m_α > m_p ≈ m_n > m_e, so λ_α < λ_p = λ_n < λ_e.

questions.q: An electron, a proton and an α-particle have the same momentum. Their de Broglie wavelengths are related as —
questions.answer: B
questions.work: λ = h/p; the same p gives the same λ.

questions.q: The momentum of a photon of frequency ν is —
questions.answer: B

questions.q: The moving mass of a photon is —
questions.answer: D

questions.q: The graph of the number of photoelectrons emitted against the intensity of incident light is —
options: a straight line through the origin
questions.answer: A

questions.q: Photons of 5 eV fall on a metal of work function 2.3 eV. The maximum kinetic energy of the photoelectrons is —
questions.answer: B

questions.q: Which is more likely to cause photoemission from a given metal?
questions.answer: C

questions.q: The de Broglie wavelength of a particle of mass m and charge q accelerated through V is —
questions.answer: A

questions.q: The maximum kinetic energy of photoelectrons depends on —
questions.answer: B

sections.title: Objective type questions: each has two parts of 1 mark (fill in the blanks, true/false, match or one word).

questions.q: (a) For a given photosensitive material and constant frequency, how does the photocurrent vary with intensity? (b) Show how the de Broglie wavelength of an electron varies with √V.
questions.answer:
(a) It increases in direct proportion to the intensity.
(b) λ = 12.27/√V Å, so λ against √V is a rectangular hyperbola (λ × √V = constant).

questions.q: Fill in the blanks: (a) The minimum frequency of light that can eject electrons is the ______ frequency. (b) The minimum energy needed to free an electron from a metal is the ______.
questions.answer:
(a) threshold
(b) work function

questions.q: State True or False: (a) Maximum KE of photoelectrons increases with intensity. (b) A photon has zero rest mass.
questions.answer:
(a) False — it depends on frequency.
(b) True.

questions.q: Complete: (a) Einstein's photoelectric equation: KE_max = ______. (b) The slope of the stopping potential–frequency graph is ______.
questions.answer:
(a) hν − φ (= hν − hν₀)
(b) h/e

sections.title: Very short answer questions. Answer in 30–50 words.

questions.q: Define (a) stopping potential and (b) threshold frequency.
questions.answer:
(a) Stopping potential: the minimum negative potential applied to the anode that stops the most energetic photoelectrons, so the photocurrent becomes zero (eV₀ = KE_max).
(b) Threshold frequency: the minimum frequency of incident light below which no photoelectrons are emitted from a given metal.

questions.q: Write any two applications of photocells.
questions.answer: (1) Automatic doors, street lights and burglar alarms (switching by light). (2) Reproduction of sound from cinema film; light meters in cameras; solar cells.

questions.q: Out of X-rays and microwaves, which is more likely to produce photoemission? Explain.
questions.answer: X-rays. Photoemission needs photon energy hν greater than the work function. X-ray photons have very high frequency and energy, while microwave photons have far too little.

questions.q: Radiation of frequency 5.6 × 10¹⁴ Hz releases photoelectrons with zero kinetic energy. Calculate the work function. (h = 6.6 × 10⁻³⁴ J s)
questions.answer: This is the threshold frequency: φ = hν₀ = 6.6 × 10⁻³⁴ × 5.6 × 10¹⁴ = 3.7 × 10⁻¹⁹ J ≈ 2.3 eV.

questions.q: Why does the maximum velocity of photoelectrons depend on the frequency of the incident light?
questions.answer: Each photon gives its whole energy hν to one electron. After spending φ to escape, the rest is KE: ½mv²_max = hν − φ. So higher frequency gives higher maximum velocity; intensity only changes the number of photons.

questions.q: Calculate the energy of a photon of wavelength 6000 Å in joule and electron-volt. (h = 6.6 × 10⁻³⁴ J s)

sections.title: Short answer questions. Answer in 50–80 words.

questions.q: State the de Broglie hypothesis. Derive the de Broglie wavelength of a particle of mass m and charge q accelerated through a potential difference V.
questions.answer:
Hypothesis: every moving particle has a wave associated with it, of wavelength λ = h/p = h/mv.
Accelerated through V: qV = ½mv² ⇒ mv = √(2mqV).
λ = h/√(2mqV). For an electron, λ = 12.27/√V Å.

questions.q: Give the four main observations from experiments on the photoelectric effect.
questions.answer:
(1) No electrons are emitted below a threshold frequency ν₀, whatever the intensity.
(2) The photocurrent (number of electrons) is proportional to the intensity.
(3) The maximum KE of electrons increases with frequency and does not depend on intensity.
(4) Emission is instantaneous (no time lag).

questions.q: An isolated hydrogen atom emits a photon of 9 eV. Find (i) the photon's momentum, (ii) its effective mass and (iii) the recoil velocity of the atom. (m_H = 1.6 × 10⁻²⁷ kg)
questions.answer:
E = 9 × 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ = 1.44 × 10⁻¹⁸ J.
(i) p = E/c = 1.44 × 10⁻¹⁸/3 × 10⁸ = 4.8 × 10⁻²⁷ kg m/s.
(ii) m = E/c² = 1.6 × 10⁻³⁵ kg.
(iii) Momentum is conserved: v = p/m_H = 4.8 × 10⁻²⁷/1.6 × 10⁻²⁷ = 3 m/s (opposite to the photon).

sections.title: Long answer questions. Answer in 80–120 words.

questions.q: (i) Draw a circuit to study the I–V characteristics of a photocell. (ii) How does the photocurrent vary with anode potential for radiation of the same intensity but different frequencies? (iii) How does the stopping potential change with intensity at the same frequency? (iv) Draw the graph of photocurrent against intensity.
questions.answer:
(i) The photocell (emitter and collector in an evacuated bulb) is connected to a variable dc source through a potential divider and reversing key, with a microammeter in series and a voltmeter across the cell.
(ii) The saturation current is the same (same intensity, same number of photons), but higher frequency needs a more negative stopping potential, so the curves meet the negative V-axis further out.
(iii) The stopping potential is the same for all intensities; only the saturation current rises with intensity.
(iv) A straight line through the origin — photocurrent ∝ intensity.

questions.q: Explain Einstein's photoelectric equation. How do the graph of stopping potential against frequency for two metals give the threshold frequency, work function and Planck's constant?
questions.answer:
Light consists of photons of energy hν. A photon gives all its energy to one electron, which spends φ = hν₀ to escape, so KE_max = hν − φ, i.e. eV₀ = hν − hν₀.
The graph of V₀ against ν is a straight line V₀ = (h/e)ν − φ/e.
Its intercept on the ν-axis is the threshold frequency ν₀; the metal with the larger ν₀ has the larger work function φ = hν₀.
The slope h/e is the same for every metal, so h = e × slope.
